title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 13–14
description: Reviewed B2 vocabulary for disaster and epidemic reporting, humanitarian crises, UK school stages, examination language and digital education.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided book. Teaching topics and lexical targets are source-grounded; explanatory notes, examples and Brazilian Portuguese translations are newly authored.

audit.scope: Unit 13 and 14 teaching pages, illustrations, vocabulary lists, exercise headings, language-help and common-mistake boxes, exercises, and the relevant answer key.
audit.pronunciation: Conservative broad British IPA added for reliably transcribed single terms; multiword collocations use empty IPA to avoid unsupported connected-speech transcriptions.
audit.languagePolicy: All study content in English except translations in the pt field, which are in Brazilian Portuguese.
audit.reviewMethod: Read book study pages and exercises against page renderings and checked relevant answer-key entries; audited original examples, meaning notes, item IDs, required fields and blank audio targets. No live browser test.
audit.limitations: No audio recordings are included. Live import, speech recognition and browser text-to-speech were not tested.

units.title: Unit 13 — Global problems
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 13. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Society: natural disasters, humanitarian crises and health emergencies
learningObjectives: Identify common natural disasters and distinguish earthquakes, floods, droughts, volcanoes and landslides.
Use collocations and reporting verbs for disasters: erupt, break out, sweep through, strike and spread rapidly.
Distinguish casualties, victims, survivors, refugees, migrants, and the dead and wounded.
Recognise key disease terminology and reporting expressions, including injure versus damage.

sectionsChecked: A: Disasters/tragedies; verbs connected with these words
B: Words for people involved in disasters/tragedies
Language help: injure people versus damage things

items.example: A powerful earthquake struck the coastal region overnight.
items.note: The ground shakes or trembles during an earthquake.

items.example: Several streets were closed because of the flood.
items.note: The result of water covering normally dry land; flood also works as a verb.

items.example: The farms lost most of their crops during the drought.
items.note: A long period with little or no rain; contrast a flood.

items.example: The volcano showed signs of becoming active again.
items.note: A mountain or opening that can release molten rock, ash and gases.

items.pt: fome generalizada; crise grave de escassez de alimentos
items.example: Relief groups delivered food to families affected by the famine.
items.note: A severe shortage of food affecting many people over an area.

items.example: Heavy rain triggered a landslide near the mountain road.
items.note: Earth and rock suddenly move down a slope; this is the physical sense used in the unit.

items.example: The authorities worked to slow the epidemic.
items.note: A disease outbreak affecting many people in a community or region.

items.example: An explosion damaged several empty buildings.
items.note: A sudden violent release of energy, such as from a bomb or gas.

items.pt: acidente grave; acidente de grandes proporções
items.example: The authorities investigated a major accident on the railway.
items.note: Major highlights the seriousness or scale of the accident.

items.example: The crew reported a serious incident during the flight.
items.note: An event, especially something unusual or unpleasant; not every incident is a disaster.

items.example: Investigators visited the site of the plane crash.
items.note: A crash involving an aircraft; compare the broader term accident.

items.example: Residents were told to prepare for the approaching hurricane.
items.note: An exceptionally powerful tropical storm; listed alongside tornado and typhoon.

items.example: A tornado swept through several small communities.
items.note: A rotating column of dangerously strong wind.

items.example: The typhoon forced the airport to close temporarily.
items.note: A kind of violent tropical storm; used in the unit with hurricane and tornado.

items.example: The island experienced a tropical storm last week.
items.note: A storm with strong winds and heavy rain in a tropical region.

items.example: The fishermen returned to port before the violent storm arrived.
items.note: Violent describes the intensity of weather rather than an act by a person.

items.example: Many schools had to close during the war.
items.note: An armed conflict, especially between states or organised groups.

items.example: The civil war displaced families within the country.
items.note: A war between groups from the same country.

items.example: Emergency supplies arrived after the natural disaster.
items.note: A disaster caused by natural events rather than directly by human actions.

items.example: The community came together after the tragedy.
items.note: An event causing great suffering, especially deaths or serious loss.

items.example: The volcano erupted after months of increased activity.
items.note: Used when a volcano releases lava or ash; eruption is the noun.

items.example: The eruption covered nearby fields with ash.
items.note: Noun formed from erupt; compare explode and explosion.

items.example: A device exploded in an unoccupied building.
items.note: Explode is the verb; explosion is the related noun.

items.example: The infection spread rapidly through the village.
items.note: A common verb–adverb combination for epidemics and other developments.

items.example: Without food deliveries, many people could starve.
items.note: Use starve for severe lack of food; starvation is the related noun.

items.pt: inanição; morte por falta de alimento
items.example: The charity aims to prevent starvation in isolated communities.
items.note: The condition of suffering or dying from an extreme lack of food.

items.example: The earthquake shook the office building for several seconds.
items.note: Irregular verb: shake, shook, shaken; disasters can shake a place.

items.example: Some regions have suffered from a severe drought for years.
items.note: Suffer from or suffer a drought describes experiencing its effects; the unit uses suffer its worst drought.

items.example: Fighting broke out near the border late at night.
items.note: A phrasal verb for the sudden beginning of war, fighting, fire or disease.

items.example: The storm swept through the valley before sunrise.
items.note: Often used for storms, strong winds and diseases moving quickly through an area.

items.example: After the collapse, several people were feared dead.
items.note: A cautious news-report expression; it does not mean the deaths have been confirmed.

items.example: The rescue team reported twelve casualties after the accident.
items.note: In disaster reporting, casualties may include both people killed and people injured.

items.example: The victims of the flood received temporary accommodation.
items.note: Someone harmed by an event or another person; a victim need not have died.

items.example: Rescue workers found one survivor in the damaged vehicle.
items.note: A person who lives through a disaster or dangerous event.

items.example: Everyone on the small boat survived the storm.
items.note: Verb related to survivor and survival.

items.example: Clean drinking water is essential for survival.
items.note: The noun related to survive; used in Exercise 13.2.

items.example: The family sought safety as refugees in a neighbouring country.
items.note: A person who has fled their country because of war, danger or disaster; distinguish migrant.

items.example: Many migrants move abroad in search of employment.
items.note: A person who moves to another country, often for work; the term alone does not imply fleeing danger.

items.example: The report gave a provisional figure for the dead.
items.note: The adjective dead is used collectively after the to refer to deceased people.

items.pt: os feridos (em guerra ou por armas)
items.example: Volunteers brought medical supplies to the wounded.
items.note: Wounded typically refers to people injured by weapons or in combat.

items.pt: ferido (sobretudo por arma ou em combate)
items.example: A wounded soldier was taken to a field hospital.
items.note: Compare injured, which is a broader term for physical injury.

items.example: Three passengers were injured when the bus overturned.
items.note: Use injure for harm to people; compare damage for harm to objects or buildings.

items.example: The cyclist received treatment for a shoulder injury.
items.note: Noun formed from injure; used in Exercise 13.2.

items.example: The flood damaged a bridge but nobody was injured.
items.note: Use damage mainly for things, buildings and property; contrast injure for people.

items.example: Thousands of residents fled the fighting.
items.note: Irregular verb: flee, fled, fled. Appears in Exercise 13.4.

items.example: People sought shelter in the community centre.
items.note: Seek, sought, sought; a useful combination for people escaping danger.

items.example: Several families crossed the border to reach safety.
items.note: Often used in reports about displaced people and refugees.

items.example: The animal shelter provided guidance about rabies prevention.
items.note: A dangerous viral disease that can spread through the bite of an infected animal.

items.example: The travellers asked their doctor about malaria prevention.
items.note: A disease spread by certain mosquito bites.

items.example: The public health campaign provided information about AIDS.
items.note: The syndrome associated with advanced HIV infection; the unit uses the acronym AIDS.

items.example: The clinic treated patients during a cholera outbreak.
items.note: A water- or food-borne infection which can cause severe diarrhoea.

items.example: Visitors checked whether a typhoid vaccination was recommended.
items.note: A bacterial disease that can spread through contaminated food or water.

items.example: She received an injection before travelling.
items.note: The unit mentions injections in the context of travel and disease prevention.

items.example: The village urgently needed a supply of water that was not contaminated.
items.note: Food or water can carry infectious agents; compare infected in the source's explanation.

items.example: He wore long sleeves to avoid mosquito bites.
items.note: This expression appears in the explanation of malaria transmission.

items.example: The newspaper described the outbreak as out of control.
items.note: A fixed expression in the rabies headline; describes a situation no longer being managed effectively.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: The lava moved slowly down the side of the volcano.
items.note: Hot molten rock flowing out of a volcano; a clue in Exercise 13.1.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: A strong aftershock caused further concern the next morning.
items.note: A smaller earthquake following a larger one; Exercise 13.1.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: A severe storm struck the coastline at dawn.
items.note: In disaster reports, a storm or earthquake can strike a place; strike, struck, struck.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: Residents boarded up the windows before the storm arrived.
items.note: Cover doors or windows with boards; used in Exercise 13.1 and the answer key.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: People were advised to stay indoors while the winds were strong.
items.note: A common safety instruction related to severe weather.

items.pt: tiroteio; disparos de armas de fogo
items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: Gunfire could be heard from the other side of town.
items.note: An uncountable noun for the sound or activity of guns being fired; a war clue in Exercise 13.1.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: A witness told police what happened shortly before the explosion.
items.note: Someone who sees an event; witness can also be used as a verb.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: Witnesses reported seeing a fireball near the runway.
items.note: A visible mass of flame; used as a possible clue to an explosion or plane crash.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: There was almost no vegetation on the dry hillside.
items.note: Collective noun for plants growing in a place.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: Several small streams dried up during the drought.
items.note: Describes the disappearance of water and moisture; appears in the answer key.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: The authorities issued a warning before the storm.
items.note: A notice of possible danger; relevant to the exercise headlines.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: Most residents heeded the warning and left early.
items.note: Heed is a relatively formal verb meaning pay attention and act accordingly.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: Specialists safely defused the bomb near the station.
items.note: Defuse means to make a bomb safe so that it cannot explode.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: A large oil slick drifted towards the shore.
items.note: A film or patch of oil floating on water; an exercise headline.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: The floodwater began to recede as the rain stopped.
items.note: Move back or become less widespread; the exercise uses it about an oil slick.

items.pt: bomba-relógio; situação prestes a se tornar crítica
items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: Experts warned that the unsafe system was a time bomb.
items.note: Can be literal or a metaphor for an approaching serious crisis, as in the exercise headline.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: The passengers were relieved after the emergency landing.
items.note: A landing made because of an urgent problem; averted disaster context in the answer key.

items.section: D · News reports and exercise vocabulary
items.example: The nearby streets were evacuated because of a poison gas cloud.
items.note: A cloud of harmful gas spreading through an area; exercise headline vocabulary.

units.title: Unit 14 — Education
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 14. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Education: UK stages, exams, qualifications and learning technology
learningObjectives: Describe the UK education system and distinguish nursery, primary, comprehensive, grammar and fee-paying schools.
Use natural examination expressions: take/do/sit/resit an exam, pass, fail, marks, grades and A levels.
Differentiate distance from blended learning, and understand LMS, VLE, modules and submissions.
Use compulsory education, school-leaving age and uncountable progress accurately.

sectionsChecked: A: Stages in a person’s education (UK system)
D: Talking about education: common questions

items.pt: creche; local de cuidados para crianças pequenas
items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: The baby spends mornings at a crèche near her father's office.
items.note: In this UK description, a setting for the youngest children, involving play and early learning.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: Their daughter went to nursery school before starting primary school.
items.note: A pre-primary educational stage in the unit's UK education sequence.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: He started primary school at the age of five.
items.note: School for younger children, described in this UK-based unit as roughly ages five to eleven.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: She continued her secondary education in the city.
items.note: Education after primary school; not a direct age-by-age mapping to Brazilian secondary school.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: Her brother is still at secondary school.
items.note: Generic name for a school educating older children and teenagers.

items.pt: escola secundária pública não seletiva (Reino Unido)
items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: Most children in the town attended a comprehensive school.
items.note: A UK secondary school that is not academically selective through an entrance test; contrast grammar school.

items.pt: escola secundária seletiva por exame (Reino Unido)
items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: She gained admission to a grammar school after passing an entrance exam.
items.note: In this UK context, a school that selects pupils by examination; not simply a school teaching grammar.

items.pt: conseguir admissão em; obter uma vaga em
items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: The student gained admission to the school after the exam.
items.note: Formal expression for being accepted into an institution, usually with to.

items.pt: exame de admissão; prova de ingresso
items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: The entrance exam took place in the spring.
items.note: A test used to decide whether an applicant may enter a school or course.

items.pt: escola particular tradicional e paga (no Reino Unido)
items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: In Britain, some famous public schools charge very high fees.
items.note: In British English, public school can refer to an independent fee-paying school; it does not mean a state-funded school.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: They chose a private school for their child.
items.note: The unit explains that many famous British public schools are actually private.

items.pt: escola paga; escola que cobra mensalidade
items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: The family could not afford a fee-paying school.
items.note: A school for which parents or guardians pay fees.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: The school has nearly six hundred pupils.
items.note: Common British English noun for a child or teenager attending school.

items.pt: educação em tempo integral; estudos em regime integral
items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: She remained in full-time education after turning sixteen.
items.note: A study status rather than necessarily staying at school for all hours of the day.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: Compulsory education begins at different ages in different countries.
items.note: Education required by law; the source distinguishes leaving school from continuing education or training.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: Some form of education or training is compulsory until eighteen in England.
items.note: Required by law or rule; contrast optional or voluntary.

items.pt: instituição pré-universitária para jovens de 16 a 18 anos (Reino Unido)
items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: She moved to a sixth-form college to study for her A levels.
items.note: A UK college for students roughly aged sixteen to eighteen; avoid equating directly with university.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: He hopes to continue into higher education next year.
items.note: Education at universities and similar institutions, after school-level study.

items.pt: continuar estudando ou fazendo formação profissional
items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: After leaving school, she continued with education or training.
items.note: The book notes that in England students may leave school at sixteen yet must continue education or training until eighteen.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: She chose history as one of her favourite school subjects.
items.note: A field studied at school, such as English, maths or science.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: Several students chose technical subjects alongside sciences.
items.note: One of the subject areas mentioned in the unit, alongside arts and sciences.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: Her course choices included subjects in the arts.
items.note: In the schooling context, contrasts with sciences and technical areas.

items.section: A · The education system in the UK
items.example: He was particularly interested in the sciences at school.
items.note: Subject group including fields such as biology, chemistry and physics.

items.pt: fazer uma prova; prestar um exame
items.example: All students will take an exam at the end of the year.
items.note: Common expression; do an exam and sit an exam are also used, especially in British English.

items.example: I have to do an exam on Monday morning.
items.note: Accepted alternative to take or sit an exam in the book.

items.pt: prestar um exame; fazer uma prova
items.example: She is going to sit a biology exam next week.
items.note: British English expression; do not say sit on an exam.

items.pt: refazer uma prova; prestar um exame novamente
items.example: He decided to resit the exam after receiving a low mark.
items.note: British English: take an exam again, often after failing or doing badly.

items.example: The pupils will take formal exams in June.
items.note: An organised assessment with official marking or procedures.

items.pt: prova de fim de ano letivo
items.example: The end-of-year exams cover the main course topics.
items.note: A test held at the end of the academic year.

items.pt: exame de ingresso na universidade; vestibular
items.example: She studied hard for her university entrance exams.
items.note: General expression used in the textbook to discuss entry into higher education.

items.example: She is preparing for her A levels in mathematics and chemistry.
items.note: In the UK context, qualifications commonly taken around age eighteen; the book links them to university entrance.

items.example: He needed the right qualifications to apply for the course.
items.note: An official educational or professional achievement showing completed study or assessed competence.

items.example: She received a mark of seventy-five per cent.
items.note: A numerical measure of performance in an examination; contrast a letter grade.

items.pt: conceito; nota por faixa ou letra
items.example: He earned a grade of B in the final assessment.
items.note: Often a letter or a level such as A, B+ or C; contrast numerical mark.

items.example: A minimum grade is needed to pass the course.
items.note: The lowest acceptable mark or level for passing.

items.example: He received a high grade in the language exam.
items.note: High grade usually implies doing well, though grading systems vary.

items.example: She passed her final exam on the first attempt.
items.note: The book explicitly advises pass an exam, not succeed at or succeed in an exam.

items.example: He failed the exam and arranged to take it again.
items.note: Means not achieve the minimum required grade; contrast pass an exam.

items.example: She did well in her exam because she prepared steadily.
items.note: Well is an adverb describing exam performance, not a letter grade itself.

items.example: He did badly in the exam after missing several lessons.
items.note: Opposite of do well in an exam.

items.pt: matar aula; faltar às aulas de propósito
items.example: He skipped classes and fell behind with the reading.
items.note: Informal phrase for deliberately not attending scheduled lessons.

items.example: Her sister graduated from university several years ago.
items.note: The common-mistake example connects passing exams and graduating.

items.example: The college uses an LMS to organise lessons and assignments.
items.note: Learning Management System; manages aspects of teaching and learning.

items.example: The students accessed their course materials through a VLE.
items.note: Virtual Learning Environment; a digital space for educational activity.

items.pt: ensino a distância; educação a distância
items.example: Distance learning allowed her to study without going to campus.
items.note: Learning remotely without regularly attending face-to-face classes.

items.example: The programme uses blended learning with online tasks and classroom meetings.
items.note: Combines classroom-based and online learning.

items.example: The teacher monitors the students' progress each week.
items.note: Means check or observe regularly; not mentor, which means guide or advise.

items.example: She has made a lot of progress with her pronunciation.
items.note: Progress is uncountable in this noun sense: much progress, not many progresses.

items.example: The class has made considerable progress this term.
items.note: Use make progress, not make progresses; the noun is uncountable.

items.example: The online platform records each learning activity.
items.note: Teachers can monitor students' activities in an LMS or VLE.

items.example: He signed up for an online course in computer science.
items.note: A programme of study that may consist of several modules.

items.example: The programming module lasts six weeks.
items.note: An individual part or component of a course.

items.pt: entregar um trabalho; enviar uma atividade
items.example: All students must submit their work through the platform.
items.note: Submit means formally hand in or send work to a teacher; do not say admit work.

items.example: Students can access the course wiki to check references.
items.note: Access is a verb used directly with its object; no to is needed here.

items.example: She writes a blog about her language-learning experience.
items.note: A blog can be used as part of learning activities in a virtual environment.

items.example: You can leave a voice message for your tutor.
items.note: Natural verb–noun combination for a recorded spoken message.

items.pt: idade mínima para deixar a escola
items.example: What is the school-leaving age in your country?
items.note: A standard education-system question; do not confuse with compulsory participation in education or training.

items.example: At what age do children usually start school here?
items.note: A useful phrase for asking when an educational stage begins; follow it with a complete question.

items.example: After sixth-form college, she plans to go on to higher education.
items.note: Go on to indicates progressing to another stage of study.

items.pt: continuar estudando; permanecer no sistema de ensino
items.example: He decided to remain in education after his exams.
items.note: Expression for continuing education instead of leaving the educational system.
